questions.text:
QUESTION ONE: THE RECORDER

Speed of sound in air = 343 m s-1

The recorder is a wind instrument that creates sound when air is blown across it. It consists of a tube that is open at one end and effectively closed at the other by the player's breath.

Draw a diagram of the fifth harmonic that can be produced in this instrument. Label nodes (N) and antinodes (A).
questions.expectedAnswer: Diagram showing 5th harmonic in a closed pipe (5/4 wavelength): node at closed end, antinode at open end, with 3 nodes and 3 antinodes in between.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Correct shape with correct node/antinode labels.

questions.text:
A recorder has its shortest effective length of 9.50 cm and longest of 19.0 cm.

Calculate the frequency of the fifth harmonic produced in the shortest configuration.
questions.expectedAnswer: For closed pipe, harmonics are odd: L = 5 lambda/4. lambda = 4L/5 = 4 x 0.095/5 = 0.0760 m. f = v/lambda = 343/0.0760 = 4513 Hz.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Correct wavelength. Merit: Correct frequency with working.

questions.text: Explain how standing waves are formed in a tube that is open at one end and closed at the other, and why not all harmonics can be formed.
questions.expectedAnswer: Sound waves reflect off the closed end with a 180 degree phase change (node at closed end). The reflected wave superposes with the incident wave. Only odd harmonics can form because the tube must have a node at the closed end and an antinode at the open end, which requires odd multiples of quarter wavelengths.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Wave reflects. Merit: Odd harmonics with quarter wavelength requirement. Excellence: Full explanation.

questions.text:
Some recorders can be tuned by adjusting the length. Initially the tube is too long, producing a beat of 7.00 Hz with a tuned instrument. The tuned instrument has length 0.180 m producing 477 Hz at the first harmonic.

Calculate how much the tube needs to be shortened and explain how to hear when it is in the correct position.
questions.expectedAnswer: f_beat = |f1 - f2|. 7 = |477 - f2|. f2 = 470 Hz (longer tube = lower frequency). v = f lambda, lambda = v/f = 343/470 = 0.7298 m. L = lambda/4 = 0.18245 m. DL = 0.18245 - 0.180 = 0.00245 m = 2.45 mm. As the tube is shortened, the beat frequency decreases until no beat is heard when the frequencies match.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: f2 = 470 Hz. Merit: Correct length or beat explanation. Excellence: Both correct.

questions.text:
QUESTION TWO: INTERFERENCE

A physics teacher shines a green laser through a diffraction grating placed at the centre of a semicircular screen.

nlambda = d sin theta

What does nlambda represent?

The diffraction grating has 300 lines per mm. The green laser has wavelength 532 nm.

Calculate the total number of dots seen on the semicircular screen.

Begin by calculating d.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: d correct. Merit: n_max found. Excellence: 13 total dots.

questions.text: The same laser is shone through a double slit with the same slit width but larger slit separation. Compare the patterns.
questions.expectedAnswer: Two-slit pattern: maxima further apart (larger d), less bright (only 2 slits), less well-defined (gradual change rather than sharp peaks).
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: ONE difference. Merit: Justify ONE. Excellence: Justify THREE.

questions.text:
White light is shone onto the diffraction grating. A central white region forms, with spectra on either side.

Explain why white light forms a spectrum with violet inside and red outside.
questions.expectedAnswer: White light contains many wavelengths. From n lambda = d sin theta, longer wavelength (red) diffracts at larger angle, shorter wavelength (violet) at smaller angle. So violet appears closest to the centre and red furthest away in each order.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Identifies wavelength difference. Merit: Justifies using formula. Excellence: Complete answer.

questions.text:
QUESTION THREE: DOPPLER EFFECT

Students stand on a platform listening to an approaching ambulance siren. Speed of sound = 343 m s-1.

Describe what they would hear compared to the paramedic inside.
questions.expectedAnswer: Higher frequency / higher pitch than the paramedic hears.

questions.text: Explain why the students hear a change in frequency as the ambulance approaches.
questions.expectedAnswer: The wave fronts bunch up in front of the approaching ambulance, so apparent wavelength decreases. The speed of sound remains constant. Therefore frequency increases (v = f lambda with v constant and lambda smaller).
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Wave fronts bunch. Merit: Full explanation.

questions.text:
The students hear 1350 Hz as the ambulance approaches and 1240 Hz as it recedes, at the same constant speed.

Calculate the speed of the ambulance.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Correct equation setup. Merit: One error. Excellence: vs = 14.6 m s-1.

questions.text:
The students listen to another ambulance that approaches and passes without stopping. The graph shows frequency vs position.

Explain what may be happening in Section A (approaching).
questions.expectedAnswer: The graph shows increasing frequency as the ambulance approaches. This indicates the ambulance is accelerating — as it gets closer and faster, wave fronts bunch up more, increasing the apparent frequency.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Increasing frequency. Merit: Justify with acceleration.

questions.text: Explain Point B (right in front of the students).
questions.expectedAnswer: They hear the actual frequency because there is no component of velocity toward them at that instant.
Decreasing frequency as the ambulance recedes and accelerates away. The wave fronts spread out more as the velocity increases relative to the observers.
questions.markingGuide: Achievement: Decreasing frequency. Merit: Justified with acceleration.
